reference.answer: In the United States vs. O'Hagan case, the Supreme Court set a precedent for interpreting SEC Rule 10(b) by using the "misappropriation theory." This theory states that misappropriating confidential information for securities trading purposes, in breach of a duty owed to the source of that information, requires disclosure or abstention. From a legal perspective, the rules are anything but clear outside of company insiders. However, your own admission is consistent with what anyone in the securities industry knows is true - if you trade on material non-public information, you risk being charged. It's possible to commit normal fraud all day long, and the SEC won't lift a finger, but as soon as you get within a hundred miles of an insider trading deal, they'll come down on you like a ton of bricks. It's an easy case to prove; there is no question about its illegality (even the janitor is expected to take a class on it), and the SEC was specifically set up to stop it after the Great Depression.

Do US-based companies need to comply with SEC regulations?

Yes, US-based companies are obligated to adhere to the regulations mandated by the US government, which are supervised by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). The SEC's EDGAR system contains all the necessary reports. Both foreign and domestic companies must electronically submit registration statements, periodic reports, and other forms to the SEC's EDGAR database.
What are the requirements?

The SEC defines an accredited investor as a variety of entities, including financial institutions, employee benefit plans with over $5 million in assets, certain charitable organizations, and individuals meeting specific income or net worth thresholds. There are no citizenship or residency requirements to qualify.
If a company has more than 500 shareholders, it must register with the SEC as an Investment Company. This registration brings about public reporting and additional regulatory compliance. This often leads to the practical necessity of going public with an IPO, even if it's not a legal requirement.
What is the filing requirement for them?

There are many different kinds of SEC filings with different purposes.  Prior to going public, a company has to file financial documents with the SEC. These filings are available to the public at www.sec.gov on the Edgar database. There are various types of filings, some specific to publicly traded companies and others applicable to registered corporations in general. You can find more information on different types of filings at http://reportstream.io/explore/has-form.
Is there one that is more important than the others?

Yes. Some SEC filings are more important than others. While OTC transactions of securities is not outright forbidden, there are numerous regulations issued by the SEC as a result of the 1943 Exchange Act and others that make this difficult and/or costly. Many other securities are exempted from registration thus trade in a way that could be called OTC. Different countries have variances upon US law but are very similar. Any security could be traded OTC, but law prohibits it expressly or in such a way to make it relatively expensive; further, stock options are so tightly regulated that expiration dates, expiration intervals, strike intervals, and minimum ticks are all set by the authorities.

Lending of securities is done by institutional investors and mutual funds. The costs of dealing with thousands of individual investors, small share blocks and the various screw-ups and drama associated with each individual are too high. Like many exotic financial transactions, if you have to ask about it, you're probably not qualified to do it.

First, realize that Wikipedia is written by individuals, just like this board has thousands of members. The two definition were written and edited by different people, most likely.  Think Venn diagram.  The definition for financial instruments claims that it's the larger set, and securities is contained in a subset.  Comparing the two, it seems pretty consistent.  Yes, Securities include derivatives.  Transferable is close to tradable, although to me tradable implies a market as compared to private transfers.  I don't believe there's an opposite, per se, but there's 'other stuff.' My house has value, but is not a security. My coffee cup has no value. Back to the concept of Venn. There aren't really opposites, just items falling outside the set we're discussing.  I'd caution, this is a semantic exercise. If you know what you're buying, a stock, a bond, a gold bar, etc, whether it's a financial instrument or security doesn't matter to you.

If you're talking about TRUPS (Trust Preferred securities) these are all but banned for new issuance under Dodd-Frank and other regulations. Although some companies still have outstanding TRUPS most have either matured, defaulted or been refinanced into some other form of debt. Its not really an available form of capital raising anymore.
